title: Gotama

teacherSummary.text: In the grove of Jetavana, Siddhartha and Govinda hear Gotama teach. Govinda joins the Buddha's followers. Siddhartha deeply admires Gotama but explains to him that enlightenment cannot be taught in words; each person must find it alone. Gotama warns him gently against too much cleverness, and Siddhartha leaves, feeling Gotama has taken his friend but given him himself.

It rests his case on what he saw, not on what he was taught

They largely talk past each other. Gotama answers the logical objection by changing the question: his teaching does not aim “to explain the world to those who seek knowledge”; “their goal is salvation from suffering” (Gotama, paragraph 36). Siddhartha accepts that (“You are truly right, there is little to opinions”, paragraph 37) and makes a different claim, that a teaching cannot hand over “what has happened to you in the hour of enlightenment.” Gotama never denies this. The case for a real disagreement lies in what follows: Gotama asks whether his monks should “abandon the teachings” (paragraph 39), implying that the path does lead to the goal, while Siddhartha holds that “nobody will obtain salvation by means of teachings” (paragraph 37). They agree on what a teaching is not, and disagree on whether it can still be a road.

The narration enacts the argument before Siddhartha makes it. The doctrine reaches us as a summary of “the four main doctrines” and “the eightfold path” (Gotama, paragraph 17), while the prose slows over Gotama’s head, feet and hand until it “glistened of truth” (paragraph 15). Readers, like Siddhartha, meet truth as a presence they can see rather than a doctrine they can repeat, which prepares his claim that what happened to Gotama cannot be conveyed “in words and through teachings” (paragraph 37). The limit is that the novel is itself made of words: Hesse can only point at a wordless experience with more description, so the reader must take the holiness on the narrator’s authority, much as Govinda takes it on Gotama’s.
A wholeness holding opposites that no rule can teach

In both scenes the elder lets the younger go once he sees the choice is already made. The father yields when he realizes that his son “had already left him” (The Son of the Brahmin, paragraph 47) and sends him off: “go into the forest and be a Samana” (paragraph 49). Gotama answers the announcement of departure with “As you please” (Gotama, paragraph 32) and ends the talk “with a hardly noticeable gesture” (paragraph 41). What they share is a refusal to hold him. The differences are as telling: the father consents after a night of struggle and asks to be taught, while Gotama needs no struggle and asks for nothing, which is the calm Siddhartha then wants for himself (paragraph 44). The two partings frame the first four chapters: one teacher lets him go in pain, the other in peace.
Gotama himself did not reach it through teachings
Siddhartha’s rule should apply to everyone
Bind himself to a new master

The claim mistakes his opening argument for his motive. He points to a break in “the entire eternal and uniform law of the world” (Gotama, paragraph 35), but when Gotama answers that the teaching aims at “salvation from suffering” (paragraph 36), Siddhartha concedes and gives a different reason: salvation “has not come to you by means of teachings!” (paragraph 37). The gap shows his intellect at work, while the real reason is his conviction that enlightenment must be lived alone. The claim is therefore only partly right, since the gap is a symptom of his distrust of doctrine, not its cause.
Each friend makes a choice that is truly his own, though they part ways

I read “You’ve heard the teachings, O son of a Brahmin, and good for you that you’ve thought about it thus deeply” slowly and put it in my own words: The Buddha tells Siddhartha it is good that he has thought deeply about the teachings. contentNotes.teacherNote: Teacher note on the portrait of Gotama: Hesse's Gotama is a European novelist's fictional portrait of the Buddha, not a historical record. The hero, Siddhartha, shares the historical Buddha's personal name (Siddhartha Gautama) but is a different, invented character; in the novel the two meet as separate people. The book is not a guide to Buddhist or Hindu teaching or practice, and Siddhartha's rejection of teachings (“nobody will obtain salvation by means of teachings!” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Gotama, para. 37)) is the character's view, not a verdict of Buddhism or Hinduism (Hesse, 1922/2001a; Müller, 1881/1999).
